content: 1. Prophylaxis with misoprostol should be initiated at a dose of 200 mcg orally every 6 hours with food. If the higher dose is not tolerated, it may be reduced to 100 mcg every 6 hours. The last dose should be administered at bedtime. Therapy should be continued for the duration of treatment as indicated. Refer to the mifepristone (Mifeprex) drug monograph for FDA-approved dosage regimens. 2. For intravaginal administration, an initial dose of 25 mcg (one-quarter of a 100-mcg oral tablet) may be used, followed by repeated doses at intervals not exceeding every 3 to 6 hours. Misoprostol should not be used in patients with a history of cesarean delivery or major uterine surgery. 3. For prophylaxis in postpartum hemorrhage, administer 600 mcg orally within 1 minute of delivery. For treatment, a single dose of 800 mcg orally may be given, but caution is advised if a prophylactic dose has already been administered and adverse effects are present or observed. Misoprostol should only be used in settings where oxytocin is unavailable. 4. For intrauterine fetal death in the second and third trimesters not accompanied by complete expulsion of products of conception, misoprostol may be used with caution. 5. In patients with renal impairment, use misoprostol cautiously as peak plasma concentration, half-life, and bioavailability may be increased. However, the clinical relevance of these increases is unclear. 6. Safety and efficacy of misoprostol have not been established in children under 8 years of age. For children aged 8 years and older, the recommended dose is 100 mcg orally every 6 hours. To minimize the risk of diarrhea, dosing may begin at 100 mcg every 6 hours and increase by 100 mcg per day every 3 days until the desired dose is achieved. 7. Antacids containing aluminum hydroxide or magnesium carbonate reduce the bioavailability of misoprostol acid. Magnesium-containing antacids may exacerbate misoprostol-induced diarrhea. If an antacid is required, use one containing aluminum or calcium instead. 8. Misoprostol enhances the effects of oxytocin through pharmacodynamic synergy. Avoid or use an alternative drug, especially if misoprostol is administered less than 4 hours before initiating oxytocin. 9. Common adverse effects of misoprostol include diarrhea (14-40%), abdominal pain (13-20%), and headache (2%). Serious adverse effects include anaphylaxis, anemia, cardiac dysrhythmia, chest pain, flatulence, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, hearing loss, myocardial infarction, nausea, uterine rupture, thromboembolic disorders, and bacterial infections. 10. Patients must seek medical attention if excessive bleeding occurs. Administration of misoprostol to pregnant women can cause abortion, premature birth, or birth defects. Uterine rupture has been reported when misoprostol is used to induce labor, with the risk increasing with advancing gestational age and prior uterine surgery, including cesarean delivery. 11. Misoprostol is contraindicated in pregnant women for reducing the risk of peptic ulcers associated with NSAID use. Patients should be warned of the risk of abortion and advised not to share the drug with others. 12. Adequate contraception is required for women of childbearing age. Misoprostol may cause anaphylactic reactions, chills, and unknown effects in women with severe anemia. It may also cause birth defects, incomplete abortion, premature labor, or uterine rupture if administered to pregnant women. 13. Safety and efficacy in patients with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, renal impairment, or respiratory disease have not been established. Use with caution in women over 35 years of age or heavy smokers, as these populations were not included in clinical trials. 14. Misoprostol is classified as Pregnancy Category X. It is rapidly metabolized in the mother to misoprostol acid, which is biologically active and excreted in breast milk. Although no adverse effects in breastfeeding infants have been reported, caution is advised when administering misoprostol to breastfeeding women. 15. Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E analogue that is rapidly de-esterified to its active metabolite, misoprostol acid. It replaces protective prostaglandins depleted by therapies that inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, inhibits gastric acid secretion, and protects the gastric mucosa. It may also reduce fat malabsorption in patients with significant fat malabsorption, possibly by stimulating duodenal bicarbonate production. 16. Misoprostol has an onset of action of 2-3 hours for initial acid secretion response and a duration of at least 3 hours for acid secretion inhibition. Peak plasma levels of misoprostol acid occur at 14 minutes, with 80-90% protein binding. It undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver, with a half-life of 20-40 minutes. Approximately 80% of the drug is excreted in the urine. 17. Misoprostol is not dialyzable.
